diagrams.title: Turn Eligible Accounts into Accepted Operator Revenue
diagrams.subtitle: Five operating stages connect account selection, outreach, qualification, routing, and recognized service fees.
diagrams.assumptions_note: Stage numbers indicate sequence, not conversion volume. Revenue means retainers and accepted-lead fees; client-funded advertising pass-through and the client's downstream sales remain excluded.
diagrams.caption: A lead becomes billable only under the agreed acceptance definition. Keep eligibility evidence, qualification fields, routing timestamps, and acceptance outcomes attached to the same CRM record.

stages.label: Define the commercial target
stages.value: Specify territory, buyer role, and qualifying need.
stages.detail: The founder records service territory, excluded accounts, buyer authority, minimum project fit, and duplicate rules before sourcing contacts or quoting accepted-lead fees.

stages.label: Establish contact eligibility
stages.value: Check provenance, channel rules, and suppression status.
stages.detail: Record source, collection date, permitted purpose, and channel-specific evidence. Reconcile CRM suppression with every sending inbox and calling queue before activation.

stages.label: Run identifiable outreach
stages.value: Operate authenticated inboxes with truthful sender identity.
stages.detail: Configure SPF, DKIM, and DMARC on authorized domains. Use Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 within provider limits; investigate complaints instead of rotating inboxes to bypass restrictions.

stages.label: Qualify and route
stages.value: Confirm need, fit, ownership, and appointment availability.
stages.detail: Use HubSpot or Salesforce required fields and Calendly availability to verify the buyer's request, assign an account owner, and prevent duplicate appointment billing.

stages.label: Accept, invoice, and learn
stages.value: Record acceptance evidence before recognizing lead fees.
stages.detail: Apply the signed acceptance and dispute terms, invoice earned retainers and accepted units, and report rejection reasons by source. Feed poor-fit patterns back into targeting.

diagrams.title: One Annual Cohort, Five Nested Conversion Stages
diagrams.subtitle: An illustrative 5,000-account cohort produces 60 client-accepted appointments without counting messages as separate prospects.
diagrams.assumptions_note: All stages count distinct accounts from one annual cohort; each later stage is a subset of the preceding stage. Count at most one accepted appointment per account. These are planning assumptions, not observed conversion benchmarks. Sixty accepted appointments at $1,000 produce $60,000; five annual client retainers at $73,000 produce $365,000; combined Base revenue is exactly $425,000.
diagrams.caption: Stage conversions are 40%, 10%, 40%, and 75%; total accepted yield is 1.2% of screened accounts. Retainers are a separate revenue component, not an additional prospect-conversion stage.

stages.label: Eligible target accounts
stages.value: 5,000 distinct accounts meet documented screening criteria.
stages.detail: Deduplicate company domains and legal entities, confirm commercial fit, and remove suppressed contacts before including an account in the annual eligible cohort.

stages.label: Accounts reached
stages.value: 2,000 accounts receive at least one eligible outreach.
stages.detail: Forty percent of screened accounts receive a delivered message through an eligible channel. Multiple contacts, inboxes, and follow-ups still count as one reached account.

stages.label: Positive account responses
stages.value: 200 accounts express interest in a relevant conversation.
stages.detail: Ten percent of reached accounts provide a positive human response. Exclude automatic replies, unsubscribe requests, wrong-person referrals without interest, and duplicate threads.

stages.label: Held qualified appointments
stages.value: 80 accounts complete conversations meeting the qualification rubric.
stages.detail: Forty percent of positive accounts attend a conversation with verified territory, commercial need, and buyer role. Exclude cancellations, no-shows, and merely booked meetings.

stages.label: Client-accepted appointments
stages.value: 60 accounts produce accepted units worth $60,000 annually.
stages.detail: Clients accept seventy-five percent of held qualified appointments under written criteria. Bill $1,000 per accepted unit; track the twenty rejected units separately.

diagrams.title: Reconcile $425,000 Revenue to $127,500 Owner Net
diagrams.subtitle: Six bars: recognized revenue, four operating-cost deductions, and a final 30.0% owner-net total.
diagrams.assumptions_note: Annual USD. The first and final bars are absolute totals; the four intervening bars are negative movements. The final bar is not another additive movement. Cost allocations are illustrative but reconcile exactly to the canonical Base scenario. The $57,500 combined software and administration budget averages $4,791.67 monthly, within the $2,000–$12,000 standing-opex range; variable delivery and acquisition costs are additional. Owner net is before personal income taxes and owner distributions; no separate founder salary is deducted in this allocation.
diagrams.caption: $425,000 − $150,000 − $90,000 − $24,000 − $33,500 = $127,500. Canonical annual scenarios remain Conservative $100,000 at 20% = $20,000; Base $425,000 at 30.0% = $127,500; Scaled $750,000 at 40% = $300,000. Conservative and Base use 1 FT + 3 C; Scaled uses 2 FT + 4 C.

stages.label: Recognized operator revenue
stages.value: Start with $425,000 in earned service revenue.
stages.detail: Recognize $365,000 of annual retainers plus $60,000 of accepted-appointment fees. Exclude client advertising pass-through, client contract value, and client sales proceeds.

stages.label: Delivery labor and fulfillment
stages.value: Deduct $150,000 for contracted service delivery capacity.
stages.detail: Budget the three contractor seats, appointment handling, quality review, and rework inside this delivery envelope. The remaining annual contribution becomes $275,000.

stages.label: Operator-funded acquisition
stages.value: Deduct $90,000 for operator-paid acquisition and sourcing.
stages.detail: Include direct prospect sourcing and operator-funded campaign acquisition expenses, not client-funded advertising pass-through. Do not duplicate standing software costs. The remaining contribution becomes $185,000.

stages.label: Software and communications
stages.value: Deduct $24,000 for the standing operating stack.
stages.detail: Budget CRM, authorized mailboxes, telephony, scheduling, and reporting subscriptions at $2,000 monthly. Keep usage charges in one cost category. Remaining contribution is $161,000.

stages.label: Administration and service overhead
stages.value: Deduct $33,500 for administration and operating overhead.
stages.detail: Cover bookkeeping, insurance, payment processing, contract review, and general business administration. This final expense deduction leaves exactly $127,500 of annual owner net.

stages.label: Annual owner net total
stages.value: Finish with $127,500, exactly 30.0% of revenue.
stages.detail: Render this endpoint as an absolute total from zero. Annual modeled expenses total $297,500, or 70% of recognized operator revenue; the founder occupies the full-time seat.

diagrams.title: Compare Accepted-Appointment Fee Hypotheses
diagrams.subtitle: Five commercial sub-niches use the same unit: operator service revenue per client-accepted appointment.
diagrams.assumptions_note: USD per accepted appointment, excluding retainers and advertising pass-through. Prices are deliberately illustrative quote hypotheses, not market averages or incremental revenue to add to the scorecard. Only the $1,000 hypothesis feeds the Base funnel. ACH and card describe collection methods; processing expenses belong in costs and do not change the gross-fee comparison.
diagrams.caption: Validate each fee against client gross contribution, close rate, attendance, and replacement burden. A $1,000 appointment at a 20% close rate implies $5,000 in appointment fees per won client before retainers and the client's own selling costs.

stages.label: Commercial HVAC service
stages.value: $1,000 accepted appointment fee, collected through ACH invoicing.
stages.detail: Require an in-territory commercial site, relevant equipment scope, and an authorized facilities contact. Reject residential requests and emergency calls outside staffed coverage.

stages.label: Managed IT services
stages.value: $900 accepted appointment fee, collected through ACH invoicing.
stages.detail: Verify employee or endpoint range, incumbent-provider context, and a business decision-maker. Reject consumer device support and accounts below the contracted service minimum.

stages.label: Industrial equipment maintenance
stages.value: $800 accepted appointment fee, collected through ACH invoicing.
stages.detail: Capture equipment category, site location, maintenance need, and purchasing responsibility. Reject unsupported equipment and work outside the client's field-service territory.

stages.label: Contract logistics services
stages.value: $700 accepted appointment fee, collected through ACH invoicing.
stages.detail: Confirm shipment frequency, lane coverage, cargo category, and commercial procurement ownership. Reject one-time consumer moves and lanes the client cannot economically serve.

stages.label: Commercial cleaning contracts
stages.value: $600 accepted appointment fee, collected through card invoicing.
stages.detail: Verify facility size, recurring service frequency, access requirements, and decision authority. Reject residential cleaning and sites below the client's minimum monthly contract.

diagrams.title: Four Pre-Flight Checks Before Contact or Routing
diagrams.subtitle: Each check has an explicit proceed condition and an explicit stop-and-repair branch.
diagrams.assumptions_note: Numeric values identify check order, not risk scores. Evaluate each channel separately and document why an unused channel is disabled. Federal rules are the starting point; applicable state privacy, calling, and recording requirements also depend on the parties, locations, technology, and campaign facts.
diagrams.caption: Proceed only when every applicable check has evidence. Missing permission, unresolved suppression, unsupported routing, or ambiguous acceptance criteria sends the affected activity back for repair.

stages.label: Commercial-email requirements
stages.value: Proceed with truthful identity and functioning opt-out handling.
stages.detail: Apply 15 U.S.C. 7704: accurate header information, nondeceptive subjects, required advertising identification unless an exception applies, valid physical postal address, and a functioning opt-out. Honor opt-outs within ten business days; stop affected sends when suppression fails.

stages.label: Calling and recording requirements
stages.value: Proceed only after documenting the specific calling basis.
stages.detail: Check 47 U.S.C. 227, 47 CFR 64.1200, applicable 16 CFR Part 310 duties, and state calling and recording rules. Distinguish live manual calls from automated or prerecorded activity and business numbers from personal wireless numbers. Disable unsupported dialing or recording.

stages.label: Privacy and data handling
stages.value: Proceed with documented scope, purpose, and rights handling.
stages.detail: Assess California Civil Code 1798.100, 1798.120, and 1798.140 where applicable, plus other relevant state rules. Document client and vendor roles, collection notices, retention, access controls, and rights-request ownership. Stop transfers that conflict with applicable sale or sharing choices.

stages.label: Quality and commercial exposure
stages.value: Proceed with measurable acceptance and bounded delivery commitments.
stages.detail: Sign territory, qualification, duplicate, acceptance, replacement, fee, and dispute terms. Test routing capacity and assign a suppression owner. Pause the affected campaign when rejection costs, acquisition costs, or churn erase its modeled contribution.

diagrams.title: Four Core Seats, Two Explicit Scale Additions
diagrams.subtitle: Conservative and Base: 1 FT + 3 C. Scaled: 2 FT + 4 C.
diagrams.assumptions_note: FT means full-time seat; C means contractor seat, not a full-time-equivalent assertion. Each numeric value represents one person. The first four seats form the baseline pod; the final two are scaled-only additions. Do not total all six seats as Base staffing or assume identical contractor hours.
diagrams.caption: The founder remains accountable for pricing and delivery economics. Automation supports consent tracking, CRM routing, and lead-quality reporting; named people still own exceptions and client acceptance.

stages.label: Founder and commercial owner
stages.value: Core seat: one full-time owner leads commercial decisions.
stages.detail: Own positioning, sales, contracts, client relationships, contribution review, and unresolved delivery issues. At scale, delegate routine account operations to the added full-time client-success lead.

stages.label: Data and CRM operator
stages.value: Core seat: one contractor owns provenance and routing.
stages.detail: Maintain account deduplication, source records, consent evidence where required, suppression propagation, access permissions, and HubSpot or Salesforce assignment rules.

stages.label: Outbound infrastructure operator
stages.value: Core seat: one contractor owns authorized outreach operations.
stages.detail: Maintain domain authentication, mailbox configuration, provider-limit adherence, message scheduling, bounce review, and complaint investigation. Escalate delivery problems without bypassing provider restrictions.

stages.label: Qualification and call-routing operator
stages.value: Core seat: one contractor verifies conversations and handoffs.
stages.detail: Review replies, qualify commercial need, confirm calendars, route calls, and collect acceptance evidence. Track no-shows and rejection causes without billing merely booked appointments.

stages.label: Client-success lead
stages.value: Scaled addition: one full-time employee owns account delivery.
stages.detail: Join only in the six-person configuration. Own client reporting, renewal preparation, delivery commitments, acceptance disputes, and capacity planning across active accounts.

stages.label: Quality and reporting analyst
stages.value: Scaled addition: one contractor owns independent quality review.
stages.detail: Join only in the six-person configuration. Audit qualification records, reconcile accepted units to invoices, analyze acquisition cost, and identify sources creating excessive replacement work.

diagrams.title: Allocate Startup Cash Before Expanding Volume
diagrams.subtitle: Four buckets form a $20,000 planning stack, with matched $5,000 lean and $40,000 expanded allocations.
diagrams.assumptions_note: Numeric values are the four segments of one $20,000 startup budget. The lean and expanded amounts in each stage use the same 30%, 20%, 30%, and 20% allocation weights and total $5,000 and $40,000 respectively. These are alternative cash plans, not three budgets to add together or scorecard revenue scenarios. Startup cash is not a recurring annual expense total.
diagrams.caption: Reserve deployment follows evidence, not inbox count. The $2,000–$12,000 monthly operating range requires a separate cash forecast, especially because the first deal may take one to four months.

stages.label: Infrastructure and operating systems
stages.value: Plan $6,000; lean $1,500; expanded $12,000 for infrastructure.
stages.detail: Allocate thirty percent to CRM setup, authorized domains, authenticated mailboxes, scheduling, telephony configuration, and initial subscription cash. Record prepaid services separately from recurring monthly expense.

stages.label: Data and qualification development
stages.value: Plan $4,000; lean $1,000; expanded $8,000 for qualification.
stages.detail: Allocate twenty percent to permitted data sourcing, account verification, qualification scripts, and small-sample quality review. Avoid buying broad lists before validating territory fit and contact eligibility.

stages.label: Pilot delivery and acquisition
stages.value: Plan $6,000; lean $1,500; expanded $12,000 for pilots.
stages.detail: Allocate thirty percent to contractor pilot work and operator-funded acquisition tests. Measure held and accepted appointments rather than opens or raw booked meetings; stop cohorts with unaffordable rejection costs.

stages.label: Working-capital reserve
stages.value: Plan $4,000; lean $1,000; expanded $8,000 as reserve.
stages.detail: Retain twenty percent for collection delays, replacement work, and service continuity. The planning reserve covers two months at $2,000 monthly operating spend but only one-third of a month at $12,000.

diagrams.title: Build a Measurable Commercial Service in Thirty Days
diagrams.subtitle: Four weekly milestones establish scope, infrastructure, pilot evidence, and a delivery-ready operating review.
diagrams.assumptions_note: Numeric values are elapsed-day endpoints: 7, 14, 21, and 30. This sprint builds operating capability; the canonical first-deal window remains one to four months. Pilot activity uses authorized resources and eligible contacts, with spend bounded by the selected $5,000–$40,000 startup cash plan.
diagrams.caption: Finish day thirty with documented evidence and a clear continue, repair, or stop decision for each pilot cohort. Do not manufacture accepted leads, booked revenue, or a signed client to satisfy the calendar.

stages.label: Days 1-7
stages.value: Choose one niche and write the acceptance contract.
stages.detail: Select territory and buyer profile; interview prospective clients; define accepted-appointment criteria, duplicate rules, fees, and dispute handling. Produce a channel requirements checklist and a cash forecast through the four-month first-deal window.

stages.label: Days 8-14
stages.value: Configure systems and test every suppression and routing path.
stages.detail: Authenticate authorized domains, configure CRM fields and least-privilege access, and connect scheduling and call routing. Use synthetic test records to verify opt-outs, duplicate handling, assignment failures, and evidence retention.

stages.label: Days 15-21
stages.value: Run a bounded pilot and inspect qualification evidence.
stages.detail: Activate a small eligible account cohort with explicit spend and contact limits. Review delivered accounts, positive replies, held appointments, rejection causes, and contractor time daily; repair failures before increasing volume.

stages.label: Days 22-30
stages.value: Review unit economics and prepare accountable client delivery.
stages.detail: Reconcile cohort counts, accepted units, invoices when earned, and actual costs. Demonstrate the reporting pack, assign each exception owner, and pursue a retainer under the written scope without treating pipeline value as revenue.
